notes: Neither answer gives Hormozi's Skool benchmarks (about 20% average churn, under 10% for the best groups, and the drop-off after day 90). B's 'overwhelm' quote is real (raw/yt--JLN1d1ZKUU.md:71), but B wrongly says his sources contain no benchmark. A offers a SaaS-style table that is close to the generic trap, but its cohort-tracking advice and churn-ceiling framing are more usable for someone deciding when to worry.

Both answers say to take the revenue share because the owner can shrink profit, which is the key's position. Neither mentions Hormozi's ranking of deal structures or his point about being paid in proportion to risk. B wrongly says its sources don't cover this, but it attributes the revenue-over-profit view to Hormozi directly, and its Acquisition.com quote is real (raw/yt-x3e73Qn6NOo.md). A puts made-up lines in quote marks as Hormozi's 'themes' and adds a baseline-increase idea he isn't sourced on. A's margin math is more useful, but B is more faithful about what Hormozi said.

Both answers say to bootstrap, but neither mentions his 'ignorance debt' reason or the management, technical and data debt that bootstrapping piles up. A wrongly says the sources never compare the two head-on. Even so, A's verbatim quotes check out in ./raw/ and its specifics are his. B mostly paraphrases ideas without sources, though its 'when raising makes sense' section is closer to the key's condition for raising money.

Neither answer gives Hormozi's 4-4-4 split (promotion first, then delivery, then building) or his 111 rule. A gets closer: its schedule puts the first 3–4 hours on revenue-making promotion, puts delivery after that, and it says no new products until the current one works. B's quotes check out in the sources, but it claims the sources never cover how he lays out a day. That's false, and the source it quotes from describes the exact routine.

Neither answer gets his actual view: he leans 'very close to the Ramsey side' and wants the debt paid off. A falls into the generic 'compare the interest rate' advice, but it still pushes you to kill expensive debt and keep cash reserves. B's quotes are real, but it wrongly says the sources have nothing on paying down business debt and then recommends the opposite of what he says (keep the cash for growth), so B is less faithful and more misleading.

A's main advice is a refresh schedule based on spend, which is the generic trap. Its tip to write many hooks also goes against Hormozi's 'three hooks, just run the winners'. B gets his position right: keep running a winner until something beats it, with no calendar. Its quotes ('use it to death', 'grabbed basically every hook') check out. But B wrongly says the sources have nothing on the topic and misses the specifics in yt-MH-IMJxbUY4: one copy run for 6 months, three hooks, and changing the creative instead of the copy.

Both say to raise prices. A's break-even math (+10% still pays down to a ~69% close rate) comes close to Hormozi's actual 65%/25% reasoning and is easier to act on, though its '40–60% healthy close rate' figure has no source. B's quotes check out in raw/, but it wrongly says the sources have no close-rate-as-price-signal quote, and it drifts into 10x tiers. Neither answer mentions the point that a higher price raises customer conviction.

Both answers get the main call right: no ads yet, keep knocking doors. Both also miss Hormozi's real point, which is to build the business on high-volume repairs priced at $2.5-5k, with an upsell menu, a membership and a speed fee; instead they treat repairs only as a way into replacements. B wins because its reasoning rests on Hormozi quotes that appear in the sources, while A slips into generic advice like referral programs and LTV:CAC rules of thumb.

Both answers say to hold off on new channels. A puts creative volume, angles and ad production first, which is closer to the key's point that creative is the real cap. B treats the wall mainly as a money-model problem and mentions creative only as a side case. B's quotes check out in the sources, but they support a different diagnosis from the one in the key.

A gets Hormozi's core position: overwhelm drives churn, so cut rather than add. It backs this with real quotes I checked in ./raw/, including the Skool Games story and the cut from three calls a week to one. It misses the cheaper tier for ideal customers and the annual plan. B mentions a downgrade tier and an annual discount, but the rest is generic retention advice with few specifics from Hormozi.
